script_en:
Find somewhere to sit. You don't need to sit perfectly — just somewhere you won't have to move for a while. Let your hands rest wherever they fall.

You don't have to do anything with what you're carrying right now. Not yet. This is just a few minutes to be with it — not fix it, not understand it, not make it mean something. Just be with it.

Notice where grief lives in your body right now. Some people feel it in the chest — a weight, a tightness, something that makes breathing feel like an effort. Some feel it in the throat. Some in the stomach. Some feel it nowhere specific, just everywhere, a kind of grey that has soaked through everything.

Wherever it is — just let it be there. You don't have to push it away. You don't have to lean into it either. You can just... notice it exists.

Think for a moment about what you're grieving. Not to relive the pain — just to name it, quietly, to yourself. What was lost? A person. A relationship. A version of a future you had already imagined. A time in your life that's over. Name it without judgment.

That thing mattered. Of course it did. The ache you feel is exactly proportional to how much it mattered. Grief isn't something that goes wrong — it's what love looks like when it no longer has anywhere to go. And that's not a problem to solve. That's something to respect.

Let yourself breathe now. A slow breath in — not forced, just natural. And a slow breath out. Notice how even now, your body knows how to breathe. Even in grief, your lungs keep working. Your heart keeps beating. Something in you is stubbornly, quietly alive.

This doesn't mean you have to feel grateful for being alive. You don't. But it's worth noticing — your body is still taking care of you, even when you're not particularly interested in being taken care of.

If there are tears, let them come. Tears aren't weakness — they're your body saying this mattered enough to produce a physical response. That's not embarrassing. That's human.

If there aren't tears, that's also fine. Grief doesn't always show up as crying. Sometimes it shows up as numbness. Sometimes as irritability. Sometimes as the strange flatness where nothing feels real. All of it counts. All of it is grief.

Spend a moment — just a moment — holding a small image of what you're grieving. Not the worst moment. Not the last moment. Just something ordinary. A small, everyday thing about what was. A laugh. A habit. A way someone used to say your name.

Let yourself miss it.

You're allowed to miss it.

Now, gently, let that image soften. Not disappear — you don't have to let it go today. Just soften, like something you set down without dropping. It will still be there when you come back to it.

Return to your breath. Return to your body in the room. Feel the weight of yourself in the chair, on the floor, wherever you are. You are here. You are still here.

That's enough for right now. That's more than enough.

Sit down. Wherever you are right now.

You probably know what I'm going to say: breathe. And you're probably already tired of being told to breathe when what you actually want is for this feeling to stop. That makes sense.

So let's not pretend this is going to fix anything in the next eight minutes. It won't. What it can do is give you somewhere to put the feeling — not permanently, just for a little while. A container. A place to set it down without it eating you alive.

Bring your attention to your chest. Right there in the centre, or slightly left of centre. What's there? For a lot of people, heartbreak — actual, physical heartbreak — feels like pressure. Like something is pushing on the inside of your ribs, trying to get out. Or like a hollow spot that feels louder than it should.

Let yourself feel whatever is there. Don't name it yet. Just feel the physical sensation — not the story, not the memories, not the reasons — just the raw texture of what's happening in your body right now.

Now name it. One word. Just one. Tender. Hollow. Aching. Tight. Bruised. Whatever word fits.

Say it quietly to yourself: this is ___.

Nothing more is required of that word. You don't have to analyse it. You don't have to decide what it means about you or about them or about what you should do next. Just the word. Just the acknowledgement that something real is happening here.

This thing that happened to you — it's a loss. Even if people around you have said things like you'll find someone else or it was for the best. Maybe both of those things will turn out to be true. But right now, in this moment, none of that matters. Right now, something you loved is gone. And that's a loss, and losses hurt, and you don't need to rush past that to get to the wisdom of it.

Let yourself breathe into the place in your chest where it hurts. Breathe in — not to push the pain away — but to acknowledge it. You are here. I am breathing through you. I am still functioning around you.

And breathe out — not to release or let go, not right now — just to exhale. Just to let the breath finish its cycle.

You don't have to be okay. You don't have to have a plan. You don't have to know what you're going to do next week or next month. You just have to get through today. And you're doing that. Right now, reading this, sitting where you are — you're doing that.

The weight in your chest will shift. Not today, maybe not this week. But it will shift. Not because time heals everything — that's too neat. But because you will change, and what you carry will change with you.

For now, just this. Your breath. Your body. The ache that means you loved something real.

That's not nothing. That's actually everything.

Before we begin: anger is not the problem. I want to say that clearly, because a lot of meditation spaces will tell you to calm down, breathe it away, find the peace underneath. That's fine sometimes. But sometimes what you need is someone to first acknowledge — yes, you're angry, and you have every right to be angry.

So: you're angry. That's where we start.

Find a way to sit that feels strong, not soft. Sit upright if you can. Let your feet be flat on the floor. Feel some version of groundedness — not relaxation, groundedness. There's a difference. You can be grounded and furious at the same time.

Bring your attention to where anger lives in your body. For most people it's the jaw, the shoulders, the chest, or the fists — hands that want to close. Where is it for you right now? Don't soften it. Just locate it.

Good. Now take one breath in — and this time, breathe in the anger. Actually let yourself inhale it. Let it fill you. Anger is energy. It's not a foreign substance in your body, it's your own energy routed through a specific channel. It's information. It's saying: something here is not okay.

And on the exhale — don't release it. Not yet. Just let the breath out, and let the anger stay exactly where it is.

Now ask it one question. Not out loud. Just internally. Just ask: what are you protecting?

Anger is almost always protecting something. A value that's been violated. A boundary that's been crossed. A person — maybe you, maybe someone you love — that's been harmed or dismissed or treated as less than they are. Ask: what are you protecting?

Let the answer come, if it comes. It might be a word. It might be an image. It might be a feeling. Don't force it. Just hold the question open.

Whatever you find underneath the anger — that's what matters. That's the real signal. The anger is the messenger. What's the message?

You don't have to do anything with it right now. You don't have to make a decision, write an email, have a confrontation, or figure anything out. That can come later. Right now, you're just listening to what your own anger is trying to tell you.

Take another breath. A little slower this time. Not to calm down — just to create a tiny bit of space between you and the feeling. You are not your anger. Your anger is something you're experiencing, not something you are.

Notice: you have been carrying this. It takes energy. Let yourself acknowledge that this is work — holding this much feeling, trying to figure out what to do with it, trying to stay functional while something inside you is on fire.

You're doing that work. And you can keep doing it. But you don't have to be alone in it.

For now, just this: your anger is not a problem. It's data. It's pointing at something real. Trust that. Trust yourself.

Resentment is a strange thing. It often feels like holding on — like if you let it go, you'd be letting someone off the hook. And maybe that's true. Maybe they don't deserve to be let off the hook. I'm not going to tell you they do.

What this practice is about isn't forgiveness. It's not about pretending something was okay when it wasn't. It's about what happens to you when you carry this — and whether you want to keep carrying it in exactly the way you have been.

Sit comfortably. Take a moment to just arrive here.

Think of the resentment you're carrying. You know what it is. You don't have to explain it or justify it. Just bring it to mind — the person, the situation, the thing that still stings when you think about it.

Notice: what does carrying this feel like in your body? Often resentment is held in the gut — a low, slow burn. Sometimes in the jaw. Sometimes as a heaviness across the shoulders, like a coat that got wet a long time ago and never quite dried.

Wherever it lives for you, just notice it. This is what carrying this has cost you — in physical energy, in the mental space it occupies, in the small but real toll of keeping this feeling active.

I want to be honest: this doesn't mean you should let it go. Some things deserve to be held. Injustice deserves to be remembered. Harm deserves to be named. The practice here isn't about release — it's about understanding.

Ask yourself: what do I get from holding this? Not sarcastically. Genuinely. Sometimes resentment is the only form of power we have left in a situation where we were powerless. Sometimes it's the thing keeping us from having to feel the grief underneath — because under almost every resentment is a loss. A loss of trust. A loss of the relationship you thought you had. A loss of the version of yourself who hadn't experienced that yet.

Sit with that for a moment. If there's grief under the resentment — grief about who that person was supposed to be, or who you were supposed to be to them — let yourself feel a little of that. Just a little.

Now breathe. Slowly in. And out. Not to release anything. Just to breathe.

Here's what I want you to consider — and you can reject this entirely: resentment lives in you, not in them. Whatever they did, the resentment is yours. That's not fair. It's genuinely unfair that you have to carry this. But you are carrying it, and you're the one who will determine how much of your energy it takes.

You don't have to decide anything today. You don't have to forgive. You don't have to let go. You just have to be willing to look at what you're carrying — and decide, consciously, whether you want to keep holding it in exactly this way.

That's enough. That's more than most people do.

Take one more breath. Feel yourself here, in this body, in this moment. The resentment may still be there. But you're a little more conscious of it now. And consciousness is where change begins — if you want it to.

title_en: For When You've Hit a Wall
script_en:
You've hit a wall. I'm not going to pretend this is fine.

There's a particular kind of tired that doesn't respond to sleep. A tiredness that sits somewhere deeper — in the part of you that has been showing up, over and over, long past when you had anything left to give. That kind of tired. And if that's where you are right now, the last thing you need is someone telling you to push through or find your motivation or remember your why.

So I won't say any of that.

Just sit. Or lie down if you need to. There is no correct posture for being this tired.

Let your body be heavy. Don't try to feel energised. Don't try to feel hopeful. Just let yourself be as depleted as you are, without adding the extra weight of feeling bad about being depleted.

You are tired because you have been trying. That's the part that often gets missed — exhaustion is evidence of effort. You have been working, showing up, caring, trying to do things right, trying to hold things together. And it has cost you. Genuinely. Real cost.

That is worth acknowledging. Not as inspiration — not to say your sacrifice will lead somewhere. Just as fact. You have given a lot. And you're empty right now. Those two things are connected.

Breathe. Slowly. You don't need a technique — just in, and out. Let your exhale be long. Let your body drop the weight of holding itself upright, just a little.

I want you to notice: even now, at the bottom of this, your body is doing things without you. Your heart is beating. Your lungs are working. Your cells are running their quiet, automatic processes. There is something in you that does not get tired. It doesn't feel amazing right now — I know — but it's there. A floor under the exhaustion.

You don't have to feel grateful for it. You don't have to feel anything. But it's there.

What would it mean to let yourself rest — really rest — right now? Not just sleep, but permission to stop. Permission to not solve anything for the next hour. To not check anything or fix anything or figure anything out. Just to exist in this body, in this moment, without an agenda.

You're allowed to stop. Even if things aren't resolved. Even if you don't have a plan. Even if stopping feels irresponsible.

You are not a machine. Machines can run continuously. You cannot. And the fact that you've been running this long — past your own limits — is not a virtue. It's just a fact. And now you're here.

One more slow breath out. Let your shoulders drop. Let your jaw unclench, if it's clenched.

You hit a wall. That happens. It doesn't mean you're broken. It means you're human, and humans run out. And when we run out, the only thing to do is stop and let the tank refill.

The wall is not the end. It's just where you rest.

title_en: The Thing You Did That You Regret
script_en:
There's something you did, or didn't do. Something you said, or didn't say. And it lives in you — not always loudly, but reliably. It comes up when you're trying to sleep, or in a quiet moment when nothing is distracting you. You know what it is. I don't need to know what it is.

Sit with me for a moment, around this thing.

Regret is a particular kind of pain because it comes with a time stamp. It has a before and an after. There was a version of you before this thing happened — before you did it or failed to do it — and a version of you after. And the after-you has to live with the knowledge of the before.

Here's what I want to say about that: you couldn't have been a different person in that moment. I know that sounds like an excuse, and I want to be precise about what I mean. It's not that you didn't have a choice. Maybe you did. But you made the choice you made with the understanding you had, the state you were in, the pressures you were under, the fears you were carrying. The person who made that choice was real and human and doing something that made sense to them at the time, even if it doesn't make sense to you now.

That doesn't mean it wasn't wrong. It might have been wrong. The wrongness and the humanness can both be true.

Breathe for a moment. Slow, easy breath.

Now ask yourself: have you punished yourself enough? I mean this genuinely. Not as a rhetorical question. Look honestly: have you carried this long enough that it's already started to change you? Have you already done some of the work of making it right — in your behaviour, in your choices, in how you treat people now?

Because at some point, self-punishment stops being accountability and starts being self-indulgence in the other direction. At some point, the guilting becomes its own kind of comfort — a way to feel like you're paying for what you did, rather than actually changing.

This isn't about getting off easy. This is about asking: what would it actually mean to make this right? And if that's possible, are you doing it? And if it's not possible — if the person is gone, the situation is irreversible — then what? Then what is the right relationship with something that can't be undone?

The right relationship is: you learn it, you carry it carefully, you let it change how you act going forward, and you don't use it to destroy yourself. Destroying yourself doesn't help anyone.

Take a breath. Feel the weight of this thing — and also the weight of the fact that you still feel it. The fact that you feel regret means something. It means you have a conscience. It means the values you violated were actually your values — not just words.

You are someone who knows when they've gotten something wrong. That's not nothing. That's actually a foundation.

From here, you can build.

script_hi:
कहीं बैठ जाओ। ज़रूरी नहीं कि बिल्कुल सीधे। बस कहीं, जहाँ कुछ देर रुक सको।

आज यहाँ कोई काम नहीं है। कोई हल नहीं ढूंढना। कोई सबक नहीं सीखना। बस इस दर्द के साथ थोड़ी देर के लिए बैठना है।

ज़रा ध्यान दो — इस वक़्त दर्द शरीर में कहाँ है? कुछ लोगों को सीने में भारीपन लगता है। कुछ को गले में कुछ अटका हुआ। कुछ को पेट में एक गाँठ सी। और कुछ को बस हर तरफ़ — जैसे रंग बदल गया हो सब कुछ का।

जहाँ भी है — वहीं रहने दो। न हटाना है, न और गहरा जाना है। बस देखना है।

एक पल के लिए सोचो — क्या खोया है? किसी इंसान को? किसी रिश्ते को? किसी ऐसे कल को जो तुमने सोच रखा था? किसी वक़्त को जो अब वापस नहीं आएगा?

बिना किसी फ़ैसले के — बस नाम दो उसे। चुपचाप, अपने दिल में।

वो चीज़ मायने रखती थी। ज़रूर रखती थी। यह जो दर्द है — ये उसी की गवाही है। दर्द तब होता है जब कोई चीज़ अहम होती है। और अहम चीज़ें जाती हैं, तो दर्द होना ज़रूरी है। यह ग़लत नहीं है। यह इंसानी है।

साँस लो। धीरे। ज़बरदस्ती नहीं — बस जैसे साँस आ रही है, आने दो।

यह देखो — अभी भी, इस सब के बीच, तुम्हारे फेफड़े काम कर रहे हैं। दिल धड़क रहा है। शरीर तुम्हारा साथ नहीं छोड़ रहा, चाहे तुम खुद से कितने भी थके हुए हो।

कोई आँसू आए तो आने दो। आँसू कमज़ोरी नहीं। वो बस शरीर का तरीक़ा है यह कहने का कि यह मायने रखता था। यह मायने रखता था।

अगर आँसू न आएं — वो भी ठीक है। दर्द हमेशा रोने में नहीं निकलता। कभी सुन्नपन में होता है। कभी थकान में। कभी उस खालीपन में जहाँ पहले कुछ और था।

एक छोटी सी तस्वीर याद करो उस चीज़ की — जो खो गई। आख़िरी पल की नहीं। कोई साधारण सा लम्हा। कोई आदत। कोई आवाज़। कोई छोटी सी बात जो रोज़ होती थी।

उसे याद करो। उसे miss करो।

तुम्हें miss करने का हक़ है।

अब धीरे-धीरे उस तस्वीर को थोड़ा पीछे जाने दो। भूलना नहीं है — बस थोड़ा space देना है। वो रहेगी। जब चाहो, वापस आ सकती है।

साँस पर वापस आओ। अपने शरीर पर। जहाँ तुम बैठे हो — उस जगह को महसूस करो। ज़मीन। कुर्सी। दीवार। तुम यहाँ हो।

तुम अभी भी यहाँ हो।

बस इतना काफ़ी है।

कहीं बैठ जाओ। अभी जहाँ भी हो।

मैं जानता हूँ — इस वक़्त किसी के साँस लो कहने से बहुत मन नहीं करता। क्योंकि जो दर्द है, वो साँस लेने से नहीं जाएगा। यह समझ में आता है।

तो यह आठ मिनट किसी को ठीक करने के लिए नहीं हैं। बस इस दर्द को थोड़ी देर रखने की जगह है — अभी के लिए।

ध्यान दो अपने सीने पर। उस जगह पर — बीच में, या थोड़ा बाईं तरफ़। वहाँ क्या है? बहुत से लोगों को टूटे दिल में सचमुच दर्द होता है — एक दबाव, जैसे कुछ अंदर से धकेल रहा हो। या एक खालीपन जो बहुत शोर करता है।

जो भी है — महसूस करो। अभी कहानी मत बनाओ। यादें मत जगाओ। बस वो physical sensation — उसकी बनावट क्या है?

एक शब्द। बस एक। दर्द। भारी। खाली। कच्चा। तंग। जो भी fit करे।

चुपचाप खुद से कहो: यह ___ है।

बस। इससे ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं चाहिए उस शब्द से।

जो हुआ — वो एक नुकसान है। चाहे लोग कुछ भी कहें। "आगे और अच्छा होगा," "यही सही था," "time सब ठीक करता है।" हो सकता है यह सब सच हो — बाद में। पर अभी, इस पल में, कुछ था जो था और अब नहीं है। और यह दुख है। असली दुख।

साँस लो उस जगह में जहाँ दर्द है। अंदर — दर्द को हटाने के लिए नहीं, बल्कि उसे notice करने के लिए। मैं यहाँ हूँ। तेरे ऊपर साँस ले रहा हूँ।

बाहर — छोड़ो। बस साँस का चक्र पूरा होने दो।

तुम्हें ठीक नहीं होना अभी। कोई plan नहीं बनाना। अगले हफ़्ते का सोचना ज़रूरी नहीं। बस आज। बस यह घड़ी।

यह भारीपन हल्का होगा। आज नहीं, शायद इस हफ़्ते भी नहीं। लेकिन होगा। ठीक इसलिए नहीं कि time heal करता है — वो बहुत easy जवाब है। बल्कि इसलिए कि तुम बदलोगे। और यह दर्द भी तुम्हारे साथ बदलेगा।

अभी बस यह — तुम्हारी साँस। तुम्हारा शरीर। यह दर्द जो बता रहा है कि तुमने कुछ असली चाहा था।

यह छोटी बात नहीं है। यह सब कुछ है।

शुरू करने से पहले एक बात: गुस्सा ग़लत नहीं है। मैं यह इसलिए कह रहा हूँ क्योंकि बहुत जगहें तुम्हें बताएंगी — शांत हो जाओ, भीतर शांति ढूंढो, गुस्से को जाने दो। यह कभी-कभी सही होता है। पर पहले ज़रूरी है कि कोई कहे: हाँ, गुस्सा है। और हो सकता है बिल्कुल सही भी हो।

तो: तुम्हें गुस्सा है। यहाँ से शुरू होते हैं।

ऐसे बैठो जिसमें ताक़त हो — मुलायम नहीं। पीठ सीधी हो सके तो रखो। पैर ज़मीन पर। कुछ देर के लिए ऐसे बैठो जैसे तुम यहाँ हो — ढीले नहीं, बल्कि मज़बूत।

ध्यान दो — गुस्सा शरीर में कहाँ है? जबड़े में? कंधों में? सीने में? मुट्ठी बंद होना चाहती है? जहाँ भी है — नरम मत करो अभी। बस locate करो।

एक साँस लो — और इस बार, गुस्से को अंदर लो। सचमुच। उसे feel होने दो। गुस्सा energy है। यह कोई बाहरी चीज़ नहीं जो तुम्हारे अंदर घुस आई — यह तुम्हारी अपनी energy है जो एक ख़ास channel से बह रही है। यह information है। यह कह रही है: कुछ यहाँ ठीक नहीं है।

साँस बाहर — गुस्सा मत निकालो। बस साँस जाने दो।

अब एक सवाल पूछो खुद से। ज़ोर से नहीं — बस भीतर: यह किसकी रक्षा कर रहा है?

गुस्सा लगभग हमेशा कुछ बचाता है। कोई क़दर जो टूटी। कोई हद जो लांघी गई। कोई इंसान — शायद तुम खुद — जिसे नज़रअंदाज़ किया गया या कम आँका गया।

जो जवाब आए — आने दो। शब्द हो, तस्वीर हो, बस एक feeling हो। ज़बरदस्ती नहीं।

गुस्से के नीचे जो मिला — वही असली signal है। गुस्सा तो messenger है। ख़बर क्या है?

अभी कुछ करना ज़रूरी नहीं। कोई फ़ैसला नहीं। कोई message नहीं भेजना। कोई conversation नहीं। बस सुनना है — अपने गुस्से को।

एक और साँस। थोड़ी धीमी। शांत होने के लिए नहीं — बस थोड़ी सी जगह बनाने के लिए। तुम अपना गुस्सा नहीं हो। गुस्सा तुम्हारे साथ हो रहा है।

यह सब ढोना थका देता है। इतनी feeling hold करना, यह सोचते रहना कि क्या करें — यह काम है। असली काम।

तुम यह काम कर रहे हो।

गुस्सा कोई problem नहीं। यह data है। यह किसी असली चीज़ की तरफ़ इशारा कर रहा है। उस पर भरोसा करो। खुद पर भरोसा करो।

कुछ दर्द ऐसे होते हैं जिनमें एक अधूरापन होता है। कोई बात जो कभी नहीं हो पाई। कोई माफ़ी जो माँगने का मौक़ा नहीं मिला। कोई "मैं तुमसे प्यार करता हूँ" जो रह गया। कोई आख़िरी बार जो जाने बिना हो गया।

यह meditation उन लोगों के लिए है जो किसी को खो चुके हैं — और जिनके दिल में अभी भी कुछ ऐसा है जो वो उस इंसान से कहना चाहते थे।

कहीं शांत जगह बैठो। आँखें बंद करो अगर ठीक लगे।

उस इंसान को याद करो। सिर्फ़ उन्हें — उनका चेहरा, उनकी आवाज़, उनका होना। अच्छे पल को। कोई normal सा दिन — बड़ा नहीं, बस वो थे और तुम थे।

उन्हें यहाँ आने दो — अपनी कल्पना में। तुम्हारे सामने। बस अभी के लिए।

साँस लो।

अब वो बात — जो रह गई। जो तुम उनसे कहना चाहते थे। चाहे माफ़ी हो। चाहे कृतज्ञता। चाहे गुस्सा जो कभी ज़ाहिर नहीं हुआ। चाहे बस: मुझे तुम्हारी याद आती है। चाहे: मैं ठीक नहीं हूँ तुम्हारे बिना।

उन्हें कहो। भीतर। या ज़ोर से, अगर जगह हो।

कहो जो कहना है। रुको मत। यह जगह safe है।

जो कहा — उसे जाने दो। हवा में। उनकी तरफ़।

यह अजीब लगे शायद — वो तो सुन नहीं सकते। और हो सकता है वो सच हो। लेकिन तुमने सुना। तुमने खुद को सुना। और कभी-कभी यही ज़रूरी होता है — कि जो अंदर बंद था, वो एक बार बाहर आए। किसी को नहीं, बस — बाहर।

साँस लो। गहरी।

अब कुछ और: क्या तुम्हें लगता है वो तुमसे कुछ कहना चाहते? यह तुम्हारी कल्पना है — पर कल्पना झूठी नहीं होती। तुम उन्हें जानते थे। तुम उनकी आवाज़ जानते थे। उन्हें बोलने दो।

वो क्या कहते?

सुनो।

जो आया — वो उनका तोहफ़ा है। तुम्हारी memory का, तुम्हारे प्यार का।

साँस लो।

यह बात अधूरी नहीं रही। तुमने आज उसे थोड़ा पूरा किया। उनसे बात हुई — अपने तरीक़े से।

वो गए, यह सच है। पर जो उन्होंने तुम्हें दिया — जो तुम्हारे अंदर है उनका — वो कहीं नहीं गया।

आँखें खोलो जब तैयार हो। धीरे से।

तुम यहाँ हो।

title_en: Shame Doesn't Get the Final Word
script_en:
Shame is different from guilt. Guilt says: I did something bad. Shame says: I am bad. That's a completely different kind of pain — and it needs a different kind of approach.

Find somewhere private if you can. Shame doesn't like audiences, and you deserve to do this without feeling watched.

Sit however you need to sit. No instructions about posture right now — just wherever you can be with this.

Bring to mind the thing you're ashamed of. You don't have to tell anyone. This is just you and the feeling. What is it? A way you behaved. Something about your body. A way you were treated that somehow became about you. A part of yourself you hide. A want or desire you judge as wrong.

Notice the physical response that comes up as you bring this to mind. Shame often shows up in the face — flushing, wanting to look down. In the chest — a collapse inward. In the urge to disappear. Notice it without fighting it.

Here is the thing about shame: it grows in silence and dies in connection. Not performance — not going on stage and confessing everything. Just connection. A witness. Even a quiet, internal one.

So let me be a witness right now. Not to the thing — you don't have to share the thing. But to you, in this moment, carrying this.

You are carrying something heavy. That's real. And the fact that you're still here, still functioning, still trying to do right by yourself and others — that's also real.

Take a breath. Slowly in. Slowly out.

Now: where did the shame come from? Not the thing you're ashamed of — the shame itself. Shame is almost always learned. Someone — a parent, a peer, a culture, a message absorbed before you were old enough to evaluate it — told you that this part of you was wrong. Unacceptable. Disgusting. Too much. Not enough.

Who told you this?

You don't have to answer out loud. But notice: it was a person, or a group of people, or a system. It wasn't the universe. It wasn't truth. It was a voice that got inside.

Here's a question you're allowed to ask: do I actually believe this? Do I, as an adult, looking at this part of myself — do I genuinely believe it makes me unworthy? Or is it just a story that got stuck?

Maybe the answer is: I don't know. That's okay. You don't have to resolve this today.

Breathe again. Feel the weight of yourself, solid in the room.

Shame wants you to hide. To disappear. To never speak of this, never acknowledge it, never let anyone close enough to see it. And sometimes shame succeeds — people carry these things alone for decades.

But you're here. You picked this up. You're looking at it.

That's not nothing. That's actually the first move.

Shame doesn't get the final word. You do.

script_hi:
अकेलापन अजीब होता है। भरे कमरे में भी हो सकता है। सोशल मीडिया पर notifications आती रहें, तब भी। लोग आसपास हों, तब भी।

यह meditation उस अकेलेपन के लिए है — जो बाहरी दुनिया से नहीं, बल्कि इस feeling से है कि कोई नहीं समझता। कोई नहीं देखता। तुम हो, पर जैसे हो ही नहीं।

कहीं बैठो। शांति से।

पहले बस यह महसूस करो कि तुम यहाँ हो। तुम्हारा शरीर। ज़मीन से जुड़ा हुआ। साँस लेता हुआ। कुछ देर के लिए — बस यह।

अकेलापन अक्सर एक चाहत है — देखे जाने की। समझे जाने की। किसी के होने की जो actually gets it. और वो चाहत बुरी नहीं है। इंसान connection के लिए बना है। यह तड़प, यह खालीपन — यह तुम्हारी कमज़ोरी नहीं। यह तुम्हारी humanity है।

साँस लो।

एक सवाल: इस वक़्त, खुद के साथ तुम कैसे हो? सोचो ज़रा — क्या तुम खुद के लिए वो presence हो जो तुम दूसरों से चाहते हो? क्या तुम अपनी बात सुनते हो? क्या तुम खुद को seriously लेते हो?

यह कोई criticism नहीं। यह genuinely ज़रूरी सवाल है।

क्योंकि बहुत बार हम दूसरों से देखे जाने की उम्मीद करते हैं — पर खुद से आँखें फेर लेते हैं। खुद को judge करते हैं। खुद की ज़रूरतों को dismiss करते हैं।

एक पल के लिए — खुद को वो दो जो तुम चाहते हो। एक हाथ सीने पर रखो। बस रखो।

कहो — चुपचाप, अंदर — "मैं यहाँ हूँ।" बस इतना।

मैं यहाँ हूँ।

यह छोटा लग सकता है। पर जब पूरी दुनिया में तुम्हें कोई नहीं दिखता — खुद का यह एक जुमला बहुत बड़ा हो सकता है।

साँस लो। हाथ वहीं रखो।

अकेलापन एक मौसम है। हमेशा नहीं रहता। और इस मौसम में, जब बाहर से कोई नहीं — भीतर से खुद को थोड़ा साथ देना शुरू करना... यह एक शुरुआत है।

एक connection जो कभी टूटती नहीं — तुम्हारी अपने आप से।

साँस बाहर। धीरे।

तुम देखे गए — अभी — तुम्हारे खुद के द्वारा।

यह काफ़ी नहीं लग सकता। पर यह कुछ है। और कुछ से आगे बढ़ा जा सकता है।
